Oral evidence - 10 Nov 2026

International Agreements Committee

Uncorrected oral evidence: Trade in a turbulent world: how should the UK deploy its trade instruments?

Tuesday 10 November 2026

2 pm

Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Johnson of Lainston (The Chair); Lord Anderson of Swansea; Baroness Anelay of St Johns; Baroness Bi; Lord Boateng; Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury; Lord German; Lord Hannay of Chiswick; Baroness Lawlor; Lord McDonald of Salford; Lord Stevenson of Balmacara; Baroness Verma.

Evidence Session No. 8 Heard in Public Questions 77 - 89

Witnesses

Sir Sebastian Wood, Chair, Chinese-British Business Council; Professor Kerry Brown, Professor of Chinese Studies, King’s College London.

USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT

This is an uncorrected transcript of evidence taken in public and webcast on www.parliamentlive.tv.

Any public use of, or reference to, the contents should make clear that neither Members nor witnesses have had the opportunity to correct the record. If in doubt as to the propriety of using the transcript, please contact the Clerk of the Committee.

Members and witnesses are asked to send corrections to the Clerk of the Committee within 14 days of receipt.

Examination of witnesses

Sir Sebastian Wood and Professor Kerry Brown.

The Chair: Welcome, everybody, and thank you very much indeed to our two guests, Sir Sebastian Wood, chair of the China-Britain Business Council, and Professor Kerry Brown, professor of Chinese studies at King’s College London.

Just to remind committee members and our guests of the context, we are writing a report on trade in a turbulent world, clearly sparked by significant tariff volatility coming from the United States, but also driven by the issues that organisations such as the World Trade Organization face, and surrounding pressures that come from trade with significant trading partners, particularly China. We are very grateful to have both of you here today to answer these specific questions, which will then feed into our report. We will start with Lord German’s question.

Lord German: Welcome and thank you very much for coming to see us today. I would like to start with a very open question, which is really to set the scene. Where would you put UK-China trade at present? The figures that we have been provided with suggest that, each year, the deficit between what we import and what we export, in both trade and services together, is getting larger. Therefore, the question you might ask, which is worth asking, is how dependent we are—and we are increasingly dependent—on trade with China. Is there a difference between consumer behaviour and trade or business behaviour in attitudes towards this? I have a supplementary, if I may, but, just to set that open picture, I would be grateful.

Sir Sebastian Wood: Thank you very much, Chair and Lord German. It is a pleasure to be here. I am here in the capacity of chair of the China-Britain Business Council, which has been in existence for 70 years. It is the principal UK-China business association, with some 300 member companies, and represents about half of the market cap of the FTSE 100.

China matters enormously in economic and business terms globally. It is now the world’s largest economy in terms of purchasing power parity, the second largest measured just on GDP, and the second largest consumer market. What interests me, given that we have a growth challenge in the UK and need to tap into sources of growth globally, is the fact that, over the last decade, roughly 30% of the total volume of global growth has taken place in that single country, China. Although, structurally, the growth rate in China has slowed down in recent years, that proportion of roughly 30% of global growth remains more or less unchanged.

It is now our third largest trading partner and our fourth largest export destination, if you include Hong Kong. We have also been the third largest recipient of Chinese worldwide investment since 2005, after the United States and Australia, so it is already very material to the UK economy.

We could perhaps talk in a more specific way about areas of particular importance and particular dependence, but I would like to quickly highlight what I see as three big strategic opportunities for UK business in the next phase of China’s development, because the trade between us at the moment is growing slightly faster than China’s overall growth rate, which suggests that we are seeing increasing complementarity between the economies of the UK and China.

If you look at China’s recently published 15th five-year plan, there are a number of areas that fit particularly well with the needs and strengths of the UK, particularly the desire of the Chinese to develop into a modern services economy and to boost services consumption in China. When they looked for a partner in Europe to be their partner of choice in industrial development in the last couple of decades, they went naturally to Germany, but we are the services superpower in Europe, and we ought to be China’s partner of choice in developing services.

The Chinese Government in particular seem to recognise the particular potential of the services relationship with us, and the two Governments have started scoping out a possible services free trade agreement between the UK and China, which, if adopted, would be the first services FTA that China has had with any major western economy, and would send a very positive signal around the Chinese system about the potential for more services co-operation between us. That is one growing area of complementarity between us.

I will just highlight one more, which is the wave of Chinese outbound FDI that we are seeing at the moment, as Chinese companies try to escape ferocious domestic competition and the overcapacity problems that exist in China, to get closer to their overseas customers and to hedge against possible tariff barriers.

This represents a real opportunity for UK services companies, which can be their partners as they expand globally, and also directly for the UK itself as a recipient of FDI, because we have many advantages in the UK. We are relatively hospitable to foreign direct investment and, if we get our fair share of that outbound wave of Chinese manufacturing investment, we will benefit from the latest technology and industrial processes, which the Chinese now have, and it will help our own reindustrialisation agenda and help us to be globally competitive as a manufacturing economy.

Professor Kerry Brown: Thanks for inviting me. I would make two comments. One is about the bilateral relationship, and the other about the broader environment. Bilaterally, the UK-China trade and investment relationship is underwhelming. In gross GDP, it is the second largest economy in the world, and yet, as a proportion of FDI, China accounted for only 0.9% of UK outward FDI stock. In terms of investment into the UK, it is only 0.1% of the total stock, so, with the stories about China buying up all of our high streets and our companies, that has just not happened. Since 2007, there has been constant speculation as to why this huge economy is not doing more here. In fact, it is probably doing less, proportionally, than it did before. There are political and other reasons for that.

In terms of company exposure—and I looked at this from only 6 November—about 9,800 UK VAT-registered companies export goods to China, and about 95,000 import goods from China. When you think that there are 2.73 million companies in Britain, that means that, in terms of exporting from China, only 3.5% of companies in Britain deal with China. The work of the CBBC is very important, because importing from China is not an easy thing to do, let alone exporting there.

On the contextual issue, although it is true that we are rising as a trading partner in terms of global ranking to fourth and third respectively, China is the largest trading partner to over 100 countries. The default now is for China to be your largest trading partner. Although the UK is exposed, it is not as exposed as others.

The final contextual point that I will make is that dependency in terms of the way in which China shapes the global architecture of trade and investment is unavoidable. China is the only country that faced down Mr Trump on tariffs by using its rare metals. It is probably important to acknowledge that it is a phenomenal capitalist. The world’s greatest capitalist now is the Communist Party of China. It delivers solid stakeholder returns for its key shareholder, the party.

It is incredibly lean in terms of its model. China’s social welfare as a proportion of GDP is about 5.6%. In Britain, it is 11%. To my surprise, in America, depending on how you calculate it, it is more. In terms of expenditure on healthcare, China spends only 5.5% of GDP, Britain 11%, and America 18%. China’s capitalist model is without social welfare costs and without labour rights, which is why the great strategic thinker, Elon Musk, likes China. Although he does not like socialist economies, he thinks that the labour environment and capitalist environment are incredibly competitive.

I would conclude by saying that the greatest challenge and the greatest issue that any economy faces with China is very simple. It can be summed up in two words: be competitive. That is all that we can do. It is incredibly competitive and, because of technology, it is about to get more competitive.

Lord German: I will just follow that up with the slightly at-variance position taken by the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee in the House of Commons, which talks about having risk-managed growth. You both portray being competitive and needing growth. I do not know whether you understand what they mean by risk-managed growth, but is it a sensible approach to be much more cautious than you might be with other trading partners?

Professor Kerry Brown: You must, of course, have risk management, but here is the paradigm challenge. If this committee were meeting five years ago, China as a technology superpower would not be an issue that we would be so exercised by. In terms of the five-year programme that Sebastian just referred to, it is now either No. 1 or close to No. 1 in terms of scientists, universities and peer-reviewed research. In almost every area in the web of peer-reviewed science research metrics, China is now producing globally important research. In terms of technology and innovation, it is a major player.

The opportunity cost is not so much that we deal with China at peril of it taking what we have, but that we need access to the things that China is producing in terms of life sciences, robotics, AI, and almost every area. That means that the risk management is not defensive. We have to go on the offensive. It is a totally different paradigm. That would be my understanding.

Lord Hannay of Chiswick: Please do not take this as a criticism of your two opening statements, but nobody could accuse either of you of not accentuating the positive. You have accentuated the positive, and I am sure that you have made a number of extremely telling points, but could you perhaps address some of the negatives?

Do you accept, for example, that China does, on occasion, subsidise its exports and produce a perfectly good case for dumping duties? Do you accept that it is probably more committed to furthering the interests of its country than a British exporter would be, who might be more interested in the business arguments? Could you address some of those arguments? I am not wishing to come from where some of the wilder assertions about our trade relationship with China come from, but it is probably not very wise to ignore the fact that there are some quite sharp negatives.

The Chair: Lord Hannay’s questions are absolutely on point, but they are slightly covered by those of colleagues as well. Maybe you could bear in mind what he has just said and, once Baroness Verma has asked her question, wrap that answer up.

Baroness Verma: It is very much the sort of question that I was going to be putting to both of you today. It follows on from Professor Kerry Brown’s comments on being competitive. On the flip side of that, they do not have demands around social welfare or labour rights in their country, so it is slightly distorting. To what extent do market distorting practices such as those in China create problems for a rules-based trade nation such as ours? Do you see this problem being resolved more so at a multilateral level, or is it going to be at a bilateral level?

Sir Sebastian Wood: Taking both questions together, there are risks and challenges in trade and investment with China. I would broadly categorise them into three areas. One would be those that relate specifically to our own national security, such as protecting critically important technology and critical national infrastructure. The second would be undue supply chain dependence for critical inputs. The third would be the risk of unfair competition, which Baroness Verma’s question highlights.

In all of those areas, the UK should act to protect itself, but in a way that is proportionate and transparent. For example, in order to protect our critical national infrastructure and ensure that our national security is protected domestically, we have certain limitations on inward investment, which are set out in the National Security and Investment Act.

All serious economies have similar measures to protect their national security, and the Chinese certainly do, but it is important that, as we apply the rules set out in the NSIA, which is being reviewed at the moment by the Government, we do so in a way that is predictable, transparent and clear, so that we do not inadvertently deter legitimate investment that would not harm our national security, and do not frighten away investors who could bring very valuable new technology and industrial process knowledge to the UK and increase our industrial competitiveness.

When it comes to supply chain dependencies, the area that we are talking about is where there is an overlap between critical inputs for our economy and undue concentration of supply, or, in the worst case, a single supplier in the shape of China or any other country. This is not just a geopolitical point. No company and no country wants to have single points of failure in critical supply chains. That lesson was brought home to us very strongly during the pandemic.

There needs to be a dialogue between business and government to identify areas where we are at risk of undue dependence or possible single points of failure in critical supply chains. The answer should be derisking and diversification rather than decoupling. If we decouple from China in those areas, we risk, in the short term, making our industry less competitive and damaging our own economy. We also risk a wider danger to our competitiveness in the long term by damaging the underlying relationship.

The Chair: I do not want to interrupt and repeat what Baroness Verma has said, but could you cover the question, which is extremely relevant, in the sense that there are gross market distortions in China?

Sir Sebastian Wood: Yes, the unfair competition point.

The Chair: It is a state-operating business. As a free trader, my initial thinking was always, “It is great if they want to work really hard for nothing and provide me with lots of cheap stuff”. That sounds like a good thing on the surface, but it is intensely distortive and very unfair. Lower standards in other countries that allow us to have cheaper imports is not something that we should necessarily triumph in.

The second point is very relevant in terms of technology. There are headlines today in the papers. There are debates in Parliament today—and I am seeing them on the screens around me—focusing on concepts such as espionage on an industrial scale and in other areas. I do not want to put you on the spot, but those are two crucial points that feed back into the trade discussions. Not to talk over Baroness Verma, but that is more the question. How do we deal with those, and could we have an assessment of their significance?

Sir Sebastian Wood: There are cases of subsidy and of preferential or cheap finance given to Chinese companies by state-owned banks and so forth. To reduce this issue of unfair competition to a subsidy debate is to narrow the discussion unduly. It is a much wider issue, which is that China has a very extensive, end-to-end industrial strategy that includes heavy investment in education, particularly STEM education. The talent pipeline pouring out of Chinese universities with STEM PhDs is substantially larger than that in the United States, for example.

Heavy investment in infrastructure and logistics makes it much more convenient and easier for industrial clusters to form themselves and then to operate. China is well on the way to becoming the world’s first electro-state, and companies have access to relatively cheap electricity. Plus, in many cases, there is direct state support for companies, although I hear anecdotally that, as China is tightening up fiscally at the moment, the Government are trying to claw back some of the subsidies that they have previously given to Chinese companies.

The problem that we face in the West is that the WTO was not really designed to deal with trade between economies that have such dramatically different basic macroeconomic models: China’s huge industrial strategy and state-directed capitalism versus more market-driven western economies.

We have had a bit of a taste of that with Germany, which had a set of policies that were designed to privilege industry over domestic consumption. There was a lot of tension even between Germany and its partners in Europe and the United States, but this is on a different level because China is so much bigger and its industrial policy so much more extensive.

In terms of what we do about it, if there is a specific infraction against WTO rules, and the WTO finds against them on a particular case, the Chinese will usually respond and try to bring themselves into compliance. The problem, though, is that a lot of what is happening is outside the ambit of the WTO rules altogether. We seem to be seeing the world moving towards a paradigm of everyone having an industrial policy. Certainly, we have seen that in the United States over the last decade, and the EU seems to be moving in the same direction. Our own Government are talking about reindustrialisation, and we have an industrial strategy now. So part of the answer is to invest in your own industry domestically.

The other part of it is to move towards more managed trade. The US and China now have a board of trade to manage tariff levels, which may or may not be—it is probably not—WTO-compliant, but they talk about and do deals on them anyway. We have the dialogue between EU Trade Commissioner Šefčovič and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, where they recently agreed an ad hoc deal with voluntary restraint on Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the EU. The UK and China have now set up a bilateral body called the trade remedies mechanism, so we ourselves have a nascent mechanism with the Chinese to manage trade.

The Chair: Thank you for that. I would like to press the case. I do not know whether my colleagues share my view, but there have clearly been distortions of trade through state action. I am very happy to have a discussion around whether that is the morally right or wrong thing to do, but we have to accept that point, Professor Brown. How do we, as a country, respond to that? I would be grateful if you could go back to the original question.

Professor Kerry Brown: On the negatives and the idea of bilateral and multilateral, we know a lot about those distortions. When China entered the World Trade Organization in November 2001, I was in the embassy in Beijing. I remember that there was a feeling that, in entering the WTO, it would make China more like us and more like a market economy, but that did not happen. In fact, it just allowed China to pump out GDP growth and to quadruple the size of its economy in 10 years. China is really good at entering these agreements and observing the letter but not the spirit.

Over the period when we were members, the EU would constantly not recognise China as a market economy, but where are we today? What did we not do right? China has not really changed. The role of the state is absolutely dominant, but that is also the weakness, because you are looking at a country that is led by leaders who believe that technology will answer everything, and we have to ask, “Will it?”

You are also looking at a model that, in terms of energy usage, is probably unsustainable. It is about okay now, but China’s hunger for energy is unsatiated. It is producing more renewable energy than the rest of the world put together, but is still 50% dependent on fossil fuels, so that is a weakness.

Then there is demographics. China’s population will probably be half of what it is today by the end of this century. Chinese leaders believe that they will solve the plunging birth rate with robotics. This is a massive social experiment that could and may well go very badly wrong.

Finally, on consumption, for the past 20 years, I have been asked and have talked about consumption in China being so low. It remains unchanged. In 1851, before a committee such as this in this Parliament, a man called Mr Mitchell said, “Britain will not be able to sell much to China because of its thrifty consuming behaviour”. Here we are, 180 years later, with the same issue, which is an issue for the Government.

Those are some pretty profound negatives, but the problem is that China’s negatives as a global power are now our negatives too. They are our challenges. If the Chinese economy collapses, it is going to, basically, bring us all down.

In terms of what we can do, I do not see how we can, bilaterally, do a great deal, which is not to undermine what you are trying to do here. It is entirely rational and important to know where we are, but we will have an impact in China only through acting in concert with others, either in the European Union or with the United States. At the moment, can we work with the United States easily? I do not know. With the European Union, we had this agreement in October that Britain would probably be pretty happy being part of, which talked about hybrids, disease control and clean energy. These things are all important to us.

The only thing that I would say is that we have to really work multilaterally, not against but with China, because of scale and because of the way in which China divides those trying to negotiate against or with it. If we do it bilaterally, I cannot see how we would really have much impact. We are just not a big enough economy.

The Chair: I might pause you there, because this leads excellently on to Lord Hannay’s question.

Lord Hannay of Chiswick: Yes, thank you very much. That covers, to some extent, what I was going to ask you. Looking at the scene now, one could say that, for reasons that are not entirely rational, we are in a period of calm in trade relations between China and the EU and between China and the United States. In the case of the United States, the President appears to be bewitched by the wonders of a strongman leader and has, therefore, called off the trade war that he kept saying he was going to wage with China. I am not saying that that is a good thing, but I doubt that the present degree of calm is easily sustainable or likely to be sustained, whether under this President, who changes his mind rather frequently, or under a subsequent, possibly Democrat President.

Secondly, the EU has called off, as it were, an immediate confrontation over hybrid vehicles with the Šefčovič agreement, but that is focused on one product and is probably not going to last for very long, so the “buy Europe” approach may lead to some rather sharp confrontations.

My question is to both of you. Where should Britain situate itself in its trade policy in circumstances where our best guess has to be that China-US and China-EU policy is going to remain pretty tense and pretty troubled? Where should Britain be in that?

Professor Brown, you began to answer that by saying that we cannot do it on our own, which is a view that I share, but we have to face the fact that the Chinese were not born yesterday. Sitting in Beijing, they will be working out how best to keep the EU, the UK and the US apart in their dealings on trade, as well as probably others such as Japan and Korea. That is a perfectly legitimate thing for them to do, but it is not in our interests.

How can we best handle this? Should we be trying to discover more common ground with the United States and the European Union on their handling of trade disputes, in the belief that, if we discover or identify common ground, particularly if it is WTO-compliant, this will have more impact in Beijing than if we are all heading off in different directions, or do we try to have a solo British response to all this and forget about what the European Union and the US are doing?

It would be good to have your comment on how we can manoeuvre in this, because, to state the obvious, as is done far too often, President Trump is going to be President of the United States for the next two years. That is just about enough to be thinking about, and nobody can expect to know anything beyond that period, but we had better think a bit about what happens beyond that period, because that is going to be extremely important for British companies and the British economy. Could you comment on how we should handle those two big areas of external tension and any others that you identify?

Professor Kerry Brown: It is quite a brave assumption to think that America will return to predictability when Trump goes. We must learn to be very wary. In Europe, we also have competition as well as alliances. China’s largest trading bloc is the Association of Southeast Asian Nations—ASEAN—with over $1 trillion in trade.

I wonder whether, looking ahead, we explore loose alliances with a way broader group of countries that have the same issues that we have with China’s distortions and its competitive strategy. I wonder whether an alliance of some sort with Latin American, African or ASEAN countries, or India, would be worth thinking about.

In some areas, we have the same worries about China exporting excess capacity or about security. At the moment, we tend to put all our eggs into the EU and the US because they are the biggest markets, but they are getting smaller. We have to be very entrepreneurial and creative in the alliances that we are talking about. After all, this is a period of increasing multilateralism all over the place, with different multilateralisms from those that we have had before, so we should consider that.

Lord Hannay of Chiswick: Surely, the reality has been that, in the first big confrontation between the United States and China, the Chinese merely shifted a lot of its investment into Vietnam, which is an ASEAN country.

Professor Kerry Brown: Yes, but, if you talk to the Vietnamese, as I did in Oxford in the summer, when they had a delegation come over, they trust China less than we do. We have to learn from these partnerships. We probably have a lot of similarity with people, even where we might not think we do, on this particular issue of trading with China, because China’s dominance is unprecedented for a country such as it is, with its system and its values. We just have to explore tactical ways of achieving what we want, which is a relationship with China where we can at least control risk but get benefits for our growth and not get eaten alive.

Lord Boateng: Professor, you say that China’s dominance is unprecedented. Is it? Did the British Empire not have a similar dominance at its height?

Professor Kerry Brown: I remember doing some war gaming with you where you were a Chinese official, and you did it extremely well.

The Chair: Maybe we should re‑enact that.

Lord Boateng: We can leave your recollections of war games behind us. Would you answer my question? What is the answer to my question?

Sir Sebastian Wood: The CBBC does not have a position on that particular question.

The Chair: Is this an anomaly or something that we have seen historically?

Sir Sebastian Wood: In modern economic terms, it is a unique, new problem that we face. That seems to me pretty clear. As I said before, we had the situation with Germany, where its economic policies were built really to service an incredibly efficient export engine. With an economy the size of Germany, you could just about accommodate that within a rules-based global trading system, although it did cause significant intra-EU and transatlantic trade tensions.

When the economy is the size of China, the problem is an order of magnitude larger. That is why we are now seeing this move away from the WTO and towards individual economies adopting their own industrial policies.

I will come back to Lord Hannay’s question, but, as we are back to the point about the distorted global trade picture and what we do about it, I will just offer a couple of quick thoughts on that. First of all, the situation will evolve. As the Chinese leadership have sought to shift capital away from the property sector, which was becoming dangerously overinvested, and into technology, they have created this technological juggernaut.

At the same time, they have also created a rather deflationary situation inside China with overcapacity. They have moved capital away from very labour-intensive areas of the economy such as the property sector, and towards relatively jobs-poor areas of the economy, such as super-modern factories with hardly any workers in them.

There is a problem with deficient domestic demand, which the party is determined to address, and you see it in its regular policy pronouncements and, indeed, in the five-year plan that I mentioned earlier. Over time, it is likely that consumption will increase as a proportion of China’s GDP, which will serve to rebalance trade between China and its partners, and will mean a growing export opportunity.

That is the first thing that we can and should do as a country to address the problem of unbalanced trade with China. We should be on an export drive to really help many more British companies address the Chinese consumer market. At the CBBC, we are trying to do that with a programme that we have running with China’s largest online retailers, JD.com, and with other big banks as partners, just to try to get more awareness of the export opportunity that is growing in China.

The Chair: By the way, I should say thank you for your work. I have seen it at first hand, and your organisation does fabulous work in promoting our exporters. Can we return to the point? Lord Hannay also wants his question answered.

Lord Boateng: I am going to have to push you a bit.

Lord Hannay of Chiswick: Hang on a second. He said that he was going to answer my question.

Lord Boateng: He has not, but he has not answered mine either.

The Chair: He is about to.

Lord Hannay of Chiswick: Mine was asked first.

Sir Sebastian Wood: Your question was about the British Empire, which I am not really an expert on.

Lord Boateng: It is not. My question is about how we in Britain should respond today. China has been Africa’s largest bilateral trading partner for 15 consecutive years. I am old enough to remember Zhou Enlai’s first visit to Africa. In your evidence to us, you have made reference to the need for what you describe as some sort of new alliance between Africa, Latin America and India.

What I have to say to you is that we have an alliance. It is called the Commonwealth, and it involves all those countries. What I want to know is how you would suggest that the Commonwealth, and the UK within the Commonwealth, respond to China’s dominance in these areas, whether by out-and-out mobilisation of our interests against its interests, or by co-operation, where we can co-operate, on the development front. If you could give us some practical suggestions as to how UK policy might assist either of those approaches, and which is most likely to be successful from the point of view of developing nations and of our own economies, that would be of interest to the committee.

The Chair: Be quite brief, and then, Sebastian, could you go back to the US and EU relationships? Who wants to take that follow-up point?

Professor Kerry Brown: Which point?

The Chair: The last point made by Lord Boateng.

Professor Kerry Brown: I have no idea whether the Commonwealth could be focused on a specific issue such as creating balanced, sustainable, equitable trading relations with a partner such as China, but we have to be open-minded now.

On China’s impact in Africa, it really depends on the country and the area. It is very complicated. To answer your question about development, China would not view development in the same way as Britain, for instance.

Lord Boateng: Where is the difference?

Professor Kerry Brown: It would view development as an economic opportunity for China.

Lord Boateng: Do we not regard development as an economic opportunity for Britain? Please, Professor.

Professor Kerry Brown: The way that we present it is that we regard it as more altruistic, I suppose, but you might be right.

The Chair: It is a good discussion to have. Sebastian, could you comment briefly on the important question that Lord Hannay asked about the US and EU in terms of our alliances and their own relationships?

Sir Sebastian Wood: I would start from the premise that, although we have been talking about south‑east Asia and Africa, the three great markets in the global economy today are the United States, the EU single market, and China. We have chosen to leave the EU. We are now an independent trading country. We have to have the best possible trading and investment relationship with all three of those markets. We cannot afford to have the United States dictating the terms of our relationship with Europe. We cannot afford to have Europe dictating in detail the terms of our relationship with China.

When you look at the US-China relationship, the source of tension is primarily about strategic competition and national security. It manifests as an effort to decouple in areas of sensitive technology. The UK has, on occasion in the past, been caught in a crossfire because of that. The Huawei case comes to mind.

All I would say is that, in future, we need to have a very forensic focus on our own national interest. We certainly should not be in the business of just copying and pasting other countries’ export controls and investment restrictions. We should always be considering our own national interests, and the economic costs and opportunity costs of doing that. Where it makes sense for us to do that, we do it, but not otherwise.

The EU-China tensions are more about industrial competitiveness and the industrial incumbents in the EU feeling threatened now by very competitive Chinese firms. We are trying to get closer again to the EU single market, and there may be pressure in some areas for us to align with EU rules, for example, on Chinese investment. We just need to be careful that, in doing that, we do not inadvertently damage areas of our relationship with China that are important to our future competitiveness.

It might be an advantage for us. Having Made in Europe status would mean that manufacturers based in the UK can export into the single market on a level playing field with other EU producers. If the price of that is the need to have local content rules for foreign investment in the UK, Chinese manufacturers may welcome that clarity. It may end up increasing our attractiveness as a destination for FDI from China, if they think, “If we invest in the UK and comply with those rules, we can be confident that we can export into the single market from the UK”.

Lord Hannay of Chiswick: You will hear quite a lot about that within about 10 days, because carbon border adjustment mechanisms are clearly going to be emerging from the meeting on 20 November.

The Chair: We do not have a huge amount of time left. I am aware that some of our guests have travel commitments. Keep your answers quite brief, if you could. We have covered a lot of ground already. I am sure some of my colleagues want to ask supplementaries.

Baroness Bi: My question touches on some of the topics that we have already been talking about. How should the UK balance its desire for economic growth through trade with China against concerns relating to supply chain resilience and strategic dependence? Linked to that, I would be interested in your thoughts about the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee’s suggestion that we establish red, amber and green zones of economic activity.

Perhaps linked to that, you probably saw the article yesterday in the FT about China experts leaving the Government. Do we have capacity? Are we able to create clear demarcations of where we have the ability to trade? I am conscious that a lot of our discussions are—this goes to Lord Boateng’s comments—relatively superficial. I worry about the depth of our understanding of how China is thinking and operating. Can we decide, in a very structural way, that there are certain areas of trade that we can participate in? Do we have the know-how to be able to do that well?

Professor Kerry Brown: It is clearly going to be a far bigger priority than ever before. Until 20 years ago China was a marginal player, and now it is central to everything. To be honest, the FT report was interesting, but we do have China experts. We do not have a huge number, but we have them.

I have to say—this is from my personal experience—that it is not easy to speak publicly. We get attacked by lobbyists. We get attacked by people saying that we are paid for by Beijing. We get subjected to freedom of information requests. We have people with strong opinions about China in Britain. Some of them are advising government, but they do not really have much knowledge. It is a complicated place that involves a lot of complicated judgments.

The strategic dependence issue is a great example. What do we do when some of the amazing pharma companies in China produce really good cures for cancer, for instance, which is very likely in the next few years? What do we do when China comes up with really important technology in AI and areas where we need access? The game is now, “How do we get access to what China has?” It is not, “How does China get access to us?”

Of course, it is still acting in espionage as an opportunist, but no country really yet has a technology transfer deal with China. The EU was a huge transferer of technology to China, with Siemens, the high-speed trains, avionics, automotive and all sorts of things. Where is the reciprocal deal where we get access to Chinese technology? That is the bit that is missing from everyone’s trading relationship with China. The EU does not have it. I do not think America has it. We are going to need technology transfer from China.

A final thing I will say is that in two key areas, AI and climate change, we do not disagree with China. This is not like the Cold War. On fundamental issues, we are probably more aligned with China than we are with the United States. Those are the areas of opportunity.

Baroness Bi: What is stopping that transfer of technology coming back to us? Is it a lack of willingness on our part or on China’s part?

Professor Kerry Brown: It would need the EU to break that one. It nearly did with the comprehensive agreement on investment in 2019, but that was not ratified. The EU is the regulator and is the great producer of the technology that China has used. We would need an alliance with the EU to get access to these phenomenal companies in China that are producing really important technology that we will need.

The Chair: I do not disagree with that.

Lord Anderson of Swansea: Gentlemen, the Lord Chairman has already mentioned the BIST Committee report in the House of Commons, talking about risk-managed growth with China and suggesting a traffic light system of red, amber and green. Does that commend itself to you? I would value your comments on that report published only on 2 November.

The Chair: Sebastian, do you want to answer that? Maybe also touch on Baroness Bi’s question about lack of Chinese skill sets in our system.

Sir Sebastian Wood: On the red, green, amber point, it is properly for the Government to respond to that. We already have something similar in the National Security and Investment Act, which sets out certain sectors where inward investment proposals would fall into the scope of sensitive sectors and would need to be reviewed. Some of those that have been reviewed to date have been rejected. A relatively small proportion have been rejected.

If you like, there is a green category that is outside those sensitive sectors; there is an amber category where things are called in for review; and then there is a red category where the investment is rejected. It is not clear to me that it is fundamentally different from the policy framework that already exists in the UK.

When it comes to avoiding critical supply chain dependencies, it seems to me that this should be about diversification and derisking rather than decoupling. The point that Kerry has already made a couple of times is absolutely right. We have become accustomed to thinking of China as a country that is catching up with the West and seeks to acquire our technology through technology transfer arrangements and by fair means or foul. That is the wrong paradigm. We need to flip that on its head. We are the catch-up country now. We need to think of ways to gain access to Chinese technology.

In negotiating FDI projects, it may be possible to negotiate arrangements that allow for the sharing of technology and industrial process knowledge. We need to take that opportunity. Otherwise, our industry will be increasingly uncompetitive globally.

Lord Anderson of Swansea: Do you share the concern already mentioned by Baroness Bi in today’s Financial Times about the exodus of China experts from senior levels of the Government? I was in the Foreign Office in 1960 when we had similar concerns about Russia and the Hayter commission recommended a massive investment at grass-roots level in respect of Russia. Should there be such an infrastructural ground level investment in Chinese studies in the UK? You have a vested interest.

Sir Sebastian Wood: My view is yes. If you look at the level of UK expertise in China, it is far higher than the prevailing level of China expertise in the UK. In the United States, there is also a need for more China expertise, but, with a number of honourable exceptions, including the professor sitting on my right, we do not have the level and depth of China expertise across our academic and think tank community that you see in the United States.

There was a very praiseworthy effort led by the former diplomat Tim Clissold to introduce an A-level on Chinese civilisation into the curriculum. He wrote an article recently in the Financial Times about it. It was very widely endorsed, including by many vice-chancellors from Russell group universities. The Department for Education, sadly, does not seem to have taken this idea on board. It would be a very good idea.

There is a structural problem with Chinese language training in schools in the UK, which is that Chinese kids who are studying in schools in the UK get a guaranteed A* if they do Chinese language. That skews the grade distribution and means it is far harder for British kids to get an A* in Chinese language. In any case, a study of Chinese civilisation, given how important China has become and is going to be in the future, seems to me to be an eminently sensible component of our curriculum for our young people in future and could easily then lead more of them to study Chinese civilisation or indeed Mandarin when they go to university. That would be a good thing.

Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury: Can I just say one very small thing? That is true of any language.

Professor Kerry Brown: Yes.

Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury: It would be true if you were Italian or French. That is pretty spurious.

The Chair: To give Sir Sebastian his credit, he was not saying that he made that decision. That was one of the rationales behind not propagating it further. We hear your points, though. We are going to come on to the last question and then take a few supplementaries.

Baroness Lawlor: We have talked enough about legally based international trade. I have not heard anything to reassure me that we will see a future where China respects—and there is sufficient evidence and a way of proving that it respects—international law in respect of trade treaties. There are subsidies. There are distortions. There is a surplus. It has all the tools. Perhaps you could comment on this view, which I take from this session.

My second point is in respect of universities. Sir Sebastian referred to catch-up; the UK is in a catch-up position. It depends on what your measures are. We are a democratic western economy, which preserves certain liberties and has a way of organising our life that is democratic, not autocratic. That means we have a different measure, which is not about catching up. We cannot catch up with China in the way that it does business.

I want to mention one other dependency, which I would like you to comment on. I am asking for three comments. It is the university sector. Our BIST Committee has put universities in the green zone. This is the zoning exercise that we have heard so much about. I am not sure that is a very sensible zone to put it in because it creates a dependency, and a dependency also distorts the economy.

If you take the universities, we have 154,000 Chinese students studying in the UK at the moment. I can assure you that that has an effect on how we teach and what we teach. It has an effect on the kind of universities we have. Britain has excelled. We have four universities in the top 10 or top 20. We are rivalled only by America. There is a distortion there.

There is also, with all due respect to Professor Brown, a distortion in your own institute. I think it is Dr—I cannot pronounce his name.

Professor Kerry Brown: Is it Ming-Wai Lau?

Baroness Lawlor: Yes. He has given a major donation, 99%, to your institute. This is not the only one. It happens all over the UK. You have Chinese institutes, Chinese this and Chinese houses. It creates a distortion, no matter how well meaning or how many critics you have. The problem for us is that that person has advocated and presses for the integration of the Hong Kong economy into the Chinese economy. That surely is not in line with Britain’s interests or its own democratic and free market ethos.

For all one says about the United States or other economies, they share an aspiration for democracy and the rule of law. Therefore, I cannot see that putting your hands up on any of these matters and saying, “We have to do business with them” is the answer.

Professor Kerry Brown: The claim about my institute is not true. Endowments are 100% from a funder. That is the way endowments work. We are very lucky to get that money. Ming-Wai Lau has never ever—I will say this on oath—told me what to say or what to think.

The problem is the funding. Where is the funding going to come from? I am afraid we were looking for funding from different places. We need to fund China studies in Britain. The Government will not fund it. It is the same with universities. I am terribly sorry, but there have been very powerful arguments made for the unsustainability of funding of universities through student fees. For a period of time, we took international students, but that is declining.

You quoted a figure of 145,000. I think it has gone down to 110,000 from China. At King’s, we are lucky in being competitive because of our global ranking, but, because of the rise of Chinese universities in global rankings, we will not get that in the future. You guys will have to come up with a way of getting funding for universities.

I would completely agree with everything you say, but where is the money going to come from for this? We do not have to deal with China. It is absolutely fine. You can make a policy decision to have nothing to do with the place, but it is a massive opportunity cost. When, as I say, Chinese companies produce really important technology in cancer and other areas, are we going to say no to that because of the issues you have talked about? It is an opportunity cost.

It is complicated; I do not deny that, but it is not something where we can just say, “No, we don’t want you” or, “Yes, we want you”. We have to balance things. That is rational.

Sir Sebastian Wood: Can I chip in?

The Chair: Can I ask you to consider in your answer a point that we keep returning to? China is a very different type of economy. You can have lots of debates about whether a certain type of economy is better than others. I personally think there has been a gross misallocation of capital. Industrial policy is a political decision rather than an economic one. It results in a misallocation of capital that is highly distortive, which is what we are seeing now as a result.

In answering the questions of Baroness Lawlor, could you touch on that distortion principle? We have not heard very clearly how we manage that and how significant you think it is.

Sir Sebastian Wood: When it comes to universities, foreign students are an enormously important education export for this country. Because China is a very large education partner, we have a large number of Chinese students. As you say, it is of the order of 150,000. We have even more Indian students. The question is, “How distortive is that?” Should we be imposing quotas on the number of foreign students from any given country into our universities? It seems to me that, economically, we are not really in a position to do that.

Chinese students bring three benefits. They bring direct revenue to the universities and their living expenses in the UK. They are worth in the billions on an annual basis for the UK economy. That is money we can ill afford to do without.

Secondly, they bring some outstanding academic capabilities, particularly in sciences and mathematics, where Chinese universities now are the strongest group of universities globally in terms of the number of papers that are cited internationally.

Thirdly, Chinese students who have been here, lived here for a few years and spent time here are more likely in the future, if they go into business, to look to the UK for partnership, business opportunities and travel.

There is a less easy to measure but probably very significant long-run economic benefit that flows from having been host to so many outstandingly talented foreign students.

Lord Boateng: As a former chancellor and now pro-chancellor of a university in the UK, I welcome Chinese students. They make a great contribution to our university. What I want to know is how we in Britain, and you in the various circles in which you move, academic and business, are encouraging and supporting British students to work in Chinese universities.

I had the pleasure of lecturing at the University of Peking when I was Chief Secretary. As chairman of the English-Speaking Union, I have been all over China listening and judging debating competitions, which ESU used to co-sponsor with China Daily, where critical thinking was actively encouraged by the ESU, China Daily and the local party secretaries.

I am not clear about what your proposals are and, indeed, what your members are doing to encourage and support British students to study in China and to encourage China to have more British students in its universities.

Sir Sebastian Wood: I am not sure. I would be happy to come back to you, Lord Boateng, on that. There may well be some large British companies that—

Lord Boateng: The fact that you cannot answer is an indication to me that our companies are doing little, if anything, actively to enable UK students to work in the very country that your council is here to promote. It does not seem to me to make much sense or carry much credibility.

Sir Sebastian Wood: Well, what I would say is that this goes to the point that was raised earlier about the lack of a significant China component in our educational curriculum in the UK. We do not have enough young people studying Chinese or studying about China at university. If we had more, we would undoubtedly have more young British people going to China to work and study.

Lord Boateng: Is it not rather chicken and egg? If, in fact, you offered more opportunity for young people to study in China, might they not do what, in my experience, having met them, bright, young and able Chinese students do, which is to urge their parents and their Government to enable them to study in the UK?

Professor Kerry Brown: Before the pandemic, the British Council had a Generation UK programme where quite a lot of young British went to China. It was very successful, but, because of the British Council’s financial problems, that does not run now. As a university, our greatest problem in getting people to go to China is that young people do not tend to want to go abroad.

When they go to China, on the whole, they are impressed and they like it, but the figures are way down on before the pandemic. It is a problem. The pandemic was a great watershed because we were really building up an accumulating interest in China and lots of people were going. There were direct flights between London and Beijing with British Airlines that do not exist now. Tourist numbers have fallen. That kind of thing really helps.

Britain produces about 260 graduates in Chinese language from its universities every year. That has not changed for about 40 years. The Swire Chinese Language Foundation supported a Mandarin excellence programme that had 15,000 young British people engaged with Chinese. They seemed to really enjoy it. At the grass-roots level, we can do stuff. You are right: that needs funding.

Lord Boateng: Is British Airways a member of the China-Britain Business Council?

Sir Sebastian Wood: It is not.

The Chair: I recommend you ask British Airways about that. It has been raised in the committee, and our businesses should certainly be supporting your initiatives.

Sir Sebastian Wood: We would welcome it if British Airways joined.

Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury: Can I ask a quick and rather political question? Going back to what we were just talking about, is there a sort of Hong Kong effect here?

Professor Kerry Brown: Is this a public hearing? Hong Kong’s perspective is an important one, and—

Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury: No, I am talking about for young people.

Professor Kerry Brown: Do you mean the young people from Hong Kong coming here?

Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury: Yes, and our young people not wanting to go to China.

Professor Kerry Brown: No, I do not think our young people going to Hong Kong has a great deal of impact.

Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury: No, sorry.

Professor Kerry Brown: You mean young Hong Kongers coming here.

Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury: I completely support and hope that we should encourage more of our young people to go to China, but I am just wondering whether there is a Hong Kong effect on their desire to go there.

Professor Kerry Brown: I do not think our young people want to go abroad, period. It is a generic issue. It is very hard. As you said earlier about learning foreign languages, the pressure on people, with the debt that they take to do degrees in Britain, means they just want to get their degree and get working as soon as possible. A year abroad is regarded as a period when they could be working and paying back the loans. It is a structural issue.

Baroness Verma: It could be that they could study there.

The Chair: Yes, it is an interesting point. I am not sure whether I agree. My children want to go to university and work in America. That is abroad. It is a question of how it is labelled. There is clearly a lot of work to do here. I do not know. We have gone over time.

Baroness Anelay of St Johns: I have a much broader question. We have heard from both our witnesses today that it is important for us not to decouple but to derisk. Let us say that I am a businessperson running a large corporation and I come to you. In derisking, what is the first risk that I should deal with?

Sir Sebastian Wood: It would be undue concentration in critical supply chains. In some cases, that may mean dependence on China alone for critical inputs. I am not necessarily making a geopolitical point. There are all sorts of reasons why having a single point of failure in a critical supply chain is undesirable for a company. That would probably be the first place to look.

Lord McDonald of Salford: My question is for Sebastian. Sebastian and I have known each other for many years. Sebastian, you run two arguments in parallel, if I may say. One is that China is fundamentally different. There are many ways that you can demonstrate that. You then say that at some point China is going to become more like us, particularly on matters of consumption. Yet, as Kerry has said, the Chinese lack of consumption is something that is historically ingrained.

All the points when we thought the Chinese might change to become like us seem to have passed without them changing. Urbanisation did not make the difference that we thought it would. Is China really ever going to need British products in the way that British industry hopes?

Professor Kerry Brown: I have written a book about the history of Britain’s relations with China for the last 400 years called The Great Reversal. British policy towards China for most of that time was that we did not want a China that was too strong because it would push us around, but we did not want a China that was too weak because it would cause problems and collapse, and we did not want to get involved with that.

That policy was probably one that we could pursue until about 10 or 15 years ago. Nothing in our history of interaction with China for 400 years shows that it is ever likely to be predictable and become like us. It has never done that. It never will do that. It will play according to the rules, but it will play with Chinese meaning. It will play with a Chinese feeling. That is always going to be the case. Otherwise, it would cease to be China.

One of our great challenges, geopolitically and economically, is not that China will be dominant and try to push us around so much, but that, as we are unable to get involved in geopolitical and other issues because of economic weakness and what have you, China will not step in. In the Middle East and other places, we are going to have a problem getting China to be a security provider when we can no longer do that. That is not today, but maybe in the future.

Our challenge is not China being aggressive and assertive. It will be in some things that are in its direct interest. Our challenge will be China just not doing anything at all.

Lord Hannay of Chiswick: We had intended to ask you, and I would now like to ask you, what role, if any, you see China playing in a future rules-based trading order. It is quite an important question. Is it currently in the interim dispute settlement procedure? I do not think so. If it is not, should we be making it a condition that it comes into a dispute settlement procedure, even if the Americans continue to stay outside it? It would help us a lot to know.

Professor Kerry Brown: The Communist Party of China is a risk management entity. It manages risk. China’s domestic issues are serious, and they are its priority. China wants predictability. It does not really want what is happening with the tariffs and Trump. It does not really want what is happening in the Middle East. China wants predictability. It is facing a demographic time bomb. It has 25% unemployment for its young. It is facing massive issues with its environment. It does not want unpredictability. To that extent, it wants a utilitarian rules-based system not underpinned by values but by functionality and use in managing risk.

Sir Sebastian Wood: There has been considerable damage inflicted on the system of rules-based international trade not just by China’s economic model but by the behaviour of the United States in the last decade or so. Paradoxically, China may feel a greater political need to position itself as a defender of the rules-based international trading system and an upholder of the WTO rules.

There was a point in my briefing, which I have failed to memorise adequately, about the Chinese engaging in discussion on the interim dispute settlement mechanism. They are engaged on that particular point.

Lord Hannay of Chiswick: They are engaged in the discussion, but not in the procedure. You are either in or you are out. The British Government decided a few months ago, having not been in at the start of the interim arrangements, that they were going to join. We now have joined, with the support of this committee, I may say. The Chinese may be talking about it.

Sir Sebastian Wood: I believe they are.

Lord Hannay of Chiswick: That does not cut a lot of grass.

The Chair: We are coming to the end of our session, I am afraid. We went on a trip to see the WTO. What came back from the discussions that we had in Geneva was that China was being quite co-operative in trying to make the WTO work. The specifics about dispute settlement process we should look into. If you have any supplementary comments to make on the discussions that we have had, we would be very keen to hear them.

Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury: You did say earlier that they tried to help, did you not?

Sir Sebastian Wood: Yes.

The Chair: We have covered an enormous amount of ground today. It might be worth us having some further thoughts. We are certainly extremely grateful to both of you for coming and talking to us. This is a very complex issue. You rightly say there are not necessarily clear answers one way or the other. That is exactly what we are trying to get our heads around on this committee: how do you deal with an economy that is very different from ours? How do we make sure that we accommodate that, but also profit and prosper from it?

Your answers have been enormously helpful. Sir Sebastian and Professor Brown, thank you very much indeed for being with us today. We are much obliged.
